641	                             25 footballers, with an average per athlete of 0.6 injuries [22]. These data are essential for
642	                             commenting on the results of our study. Our results showed that in both leagues, players
643	                             who did not contract COVID-19 had injury rates lower than the average of 0.6 reported by
644	                             Bengtsson et al. [22] in both seasons. Instead, regarding players infected with SARS-CoV-2,
645	                             they showed in the pre-COVID season an injury rate in line with the data of Bengtsson
646	                             et al. [22], while in the 2020/2021 season, after the infection, it increased significantly in
647	 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                              432
648	
649	
650	
651	
652	                             both leagues (1.44 for Serie A and 1.23 for LaLiga). The results relating to the change
653	                             between seasons within individual groups showed significant differences in both groups;
654	                             however, it should be specified that with such large samples, it is highly probable that even
655	                             minimal variations between seasons are significant (especially in the C− group which is
656	                             substantially larger than the C+ group), while if we look at the 95% confidence intervals
657	                             we see an higher increase in number of injuries in the 2020/2021 season among football
658	                             players who have had COVID-19.
659	                                   The results of minutes and matches played showed that in Serie A the players in the
660	                             C+ group, during the 2019/2020 season, played more games and in total more minutes
661	                             than the players in group C−; in the 2020/2021 season, the players in group C+ (which
662	                             contracted COVID-19 during this season), they played fewer games and in total fewer
663	                             minutes than in the previous season, on the contrary the players in group C− obtained
664	                             an increase in total games and minutes played. This could be caused both by the period
665	                             of absence linked to the infection itself and by the greater number of muscle injuries that
666	                             players in group C+ have suffered, forcing them to have a longer period of absence from
667	                             sporting activity. The same, albeit to a lesser extent, is observed in the Spanish league
668	                             showing a substantial overlap of minutes played and games played in the 19/20 season
669	                             between the two groups; however, in the following season, there was a reduction in minutes
670	                             and games played in group C+ and an increase in games played and a slight reduction
671	                             in minutes played in group C−. Our results indicate that SARS-CoV-2 infection could be
672	                             a risk factor for muscular injury, in line with the recent study by Wezenbeek et al. [15].
673	                             Multiple linear regression analysis showed that in the 2019–2020 season, the risk of injury
674	                             was significantly influenced by age, according to a previous study by Green et al. [25].
675	                             However, in the 2020–2021 season, SARS-CoV-2 infection was the variable that highly
676	                             influenced the risk of muscle injury. Therefore, belonging to the C+ group in the 2020–2021
677	                             season completely distorts the correlation between the various variables and the muscle
678	                             injury rates, becoming the main factor capable of influencing the latter. In other words,
679	                             while older players with a high number of games and playing time were at greater risk of
680	                             incurring muscle injuries in the 2019–2020 season, having contracted COVID-19 was the
681	                             primary and most important risk factor in the following season. Similarly, in LaLiga, age
682	                             was the main risk factor for muscle injury in the 2019–2020 season, while in the 2020–2021
683	                             season, the only variable that significantly influenced muscle injuries was the SARS-CoV-2
684	                             infection. The survival analysis showed that during the 2019–2020 season, the two groups
685	                             had a similar risk of muscular injury. In the 2020/2021 season, the hazard risk ratio was 3.7
686	                             to 5.1 times greater among those athletes infected by SARS-CoV-2, in line with the results
687	                             of Wezenbeek et al. [15], which reported a five-time higher hazard rate to develop a muscle
688	                             strain after SARS-CoV-2 infection. One of the reasons that could explain the age effect only
689	                             in the Italian league and not in the Spanish may depend on the fact that age is a variable
690	                             not always correlated to injury. In fact, a recent review [26] reported that age influences
691	                             athletes’ risk of calf muscle injuries, while another review [27] showed that age is not linked
692	                             to a higher risk of quadriceps muscle injury. Nevertheless, the source of our data is not
693	                             specific to the type of injury and therefore it was not possible to carry out a sub-analysis.
694	                             Future studies will have to consider this element to draw definitive conclusions regarding
695	                             the role of age on the risk of injuries.
696	                                   As discussed by Wezenbeek et al. [15], there are two possible explanations for the
697	                             correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and an increased risk of muscular injury. The
698	                             first hypothesis is that strict quarantine rules implemented during the 2020/2021 season
699	                             led to prolonged periods of abstention from training and sports participation, resulting in
700	                             muscular detraining [28,29] and subsequent loss of muscle strength [30]. Muscle strength
701	                             has been shown to be a protective factor against muscular injury [31], and the loss of muscle
702	                             strength is more significant in highly trained athletes with greater initial muscle mass [32].
703	                             The second explanation is related to the direct biological effects of the virus. SARS-CoV-2
704	                             infection causes hyperinflammation, an increase in inflammatory markers, an increase
705	                             in the neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio, and possible depletion of circulating T cells [33].
706	 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                                      433
707	
708	
709	
710	
711	                             Furthermore, the virus may cause direct damage to muscle tissue by targeting the ACE 2
712	                             receptor [17], which is widely present in muscle tissue [34]. In addition, the virus can cause
713	                             disturbances in blood flow and oxygen transport, leading to reduced muscle oxygenation
714	                             during exercise. Lower muscle oxygen saturation [35] and VO2 max [36] are possible risk
715	                             factors for muscle injury.
716	
717	                             4.1. Clinical Implications
718	                                   These results emphasize the importance of carefully considering the infection in the
719	                             decision-making process for determining athletes’ readiness to return to sport (RTS). In
720	                             fact, as already described by Elliot et al. [37] in addition to the known complications, it is
721	                             necessary to consider that COVID-19 can be responsible for musculoskeletal complications.
722	                             Therefore, our opinion is that the decision regarding the RTS should not only take into
723	                             account the remission of COVID-19 related symptoms, rest and the cessation of post-
724	                             COVID-19 drug therapy but should include specific assessment and training programs,
725	                             generally used after a musculoskeletal injury [38] and therefore consider COVID-19 not
726	                             only a risk factor but a real injury.
727	
728	                             4.2. Study Limitations
729	                                   One possible limitation of this study is that the muscle injury events were collected
730	                             from a single database, which may have resulted in some injuries being overlooked, omit-
731	                             ted, or interpreted differently, leading to over- or underestimation. Another limitation of
732	                             this study is that it was not possible to control for some factors that may have influenced
733	                             the increased risk of injury, such as previous muscle injuries in unexamined seasons,
734	                             severity of COVID-19-related symptoms, total period of quarantine and injured body
735	                             part. Nevertheless, the study’s strength lies in its design, with a largely homogeneous
736	                             population group of male professional soccer players followed prospectively with a
737	                             standardized methodology.
738	
739	                             5. Conclusions
740	                                  This retrospective cohort study, conducted on a large sample of professional male
741	                             football players from two main European leagues, has revealed a significant association
742	                             between SARS-CoV-2 infection and increased risk of muscular injury. The results of this
743	                             study show that the risk of muscular injury is 3.7 to 5.1 times higher in football players who
744	                             have been infected with SARS-CoV-2. Overall, our study highlights the need for further
745	                             investigation into the effects of SARS-CoV-2 on athletes and the development of tailored
746	                             rehabilitation protocols to ensure a safe return to play.

751	                             assisted with the interpretation. M.B. and S.M. were the principal authors of the manuscript. All
752	                             authors contributed to the drafting and revision of the final article. All authors have read and agreed
753	                             to the published version of the manuscript.

759	                             Conflicts of Interest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

 "evidenceSummary": "Laboratory study in 20 injury-free male experienced runners who ran on an AlterG treadmill at 6 to 16 km/h and 50 to 100% indicated bodyweight (36 conditions), with peak plantar force measured by Pedar-X in-shoe insoles. Peak force ranged from 1.02 BW (6 km/h, 50% BW) to 2.31 BW (16 km/h, 100% BW). In Table 1, raising speed from 6 to 16 km/h at fixed bodyweight increased peak force by about 0.75 to 1.10 BW, against about 0.19 to 0.56 BW for raising bodyweight from 50 to 100% at fixed speed.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only healthy male runners were tested, so the values do not show how injured or female athletes respond. In-shoe sensors sampled at 100 Hz capture only the vertical force, so true peaks and shear loads may be missed.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read Table 1 as a fixed rehabilitation prescription, when the authors present it as a reference that still needs clinical judgement for each athlete.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Thomson A, Einarsson E, Witvrouw E, Whiteley R. Running speed increases plantar load more than per cent body weight on an AlterG® treadmill. J Sports Sci. 2017;35(3):277-282.",
  "doi": "10.1080/02640414.2016.1163401",
  "abstract": "Twenty male runners ran on an AlterG treadmill across 36 combinations of speed (6 to 16 km/h) and indicated bodyweight (50 to 100%), while in-shoe peak plantar force was recorded.",
  "tldr": "On an anti-gravity treadmill, raising running speed loads the foot far more than raising the bodyweight setting. Treat speed changes as the big load step and bodyweight changes as the small one, and check the table before stepping up.",
  "methods": "Twenty injury-free male runners completed all 36 speed and bodyweight conditions in random order on an AlterG treadmill. Peak plantar force was recorded with Pedar-X in-shoe insoles and normalised to bodyweight.",
  "findings": "Peak force rose from 1.02 BW at 6 km/h and 50% indicated BW to 2.31 BW at 16 km/h and 100%. In Table 1, the speed effect at fixed bodyweight (about 0.75 to 1.10 BW) was larger than the bodyweight effect at fixed speed (about 0.19 to 0.56 BW). Speed related to peak force on a logarithmic curve and bodyweight on a linear one.",
  "limitations": "Healthy male participants wearing their own shoes only. Sampling at 100 Hz may miss true peaks, and only the vertical force component was measured. The abstract and Table 2 give smaller ranges (0.74 to 0.91 BW for speed, 0.19 to 0.31 BW for bodyweight) than the absolute differences in Table 1 and the discussion. The authors caution that over-ground running loads are higher than treadmill values.",
  "practicalImplications": "Table 1 can guide stepwise progression of plantar loading across speed and bodyweight combinations on an AlterG treadmill. The authors suggest walking below 6 km/h at 50% indicated BW if plantar load must stay under 1 BW early in rehabilitation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Speed steps on an anti-gravity treadmill change plantar load far more than bodyweight steps, so speed is the main lever for graded running load. The paper measured no performance outcome.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The table can help grade plantar loading during rehabilitation before running, but the paper does not show that these loads predict readiness or re-injury. It cannot be used alone to clear an athlete for sport."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/findings: reported abstract/Table 2 relative values (0.74-0.91 vs 0.19-0.31 BW) as absolute increases -> Table 1 absolute differences, speed about 0.75-1.10 BW and bodyweight about 0.19-0.56 BW ('a minimum of 0.75BW increase ... to a maximum of 1.10BW'; 'maximum of 0.54BW (for the 14 km/hr condition)')",
   "limitations: added note on abstract/Table 2 versus Table 1 discrepancy",
   "tldr: 'Use speed as the main step in progression' could push large load jumps -> speed is the big step, bodyweight the small step (text: initial small increases come from stepping indicated BW)"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Abstract, Table 2 and the discussion give inconsistent bodyweight-effect ranges (0.31, 0.329, 0.54 BW); Table 1 values were used.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

  "year": 2025,

  "doi": "10.1002/dta.3918",
  "abstract": "Market-surveillance study by European and partner OMCL laboratories of suspected illegal products containing SARMs, metabolic modulators or growth hormone secretagogues, sold as sport performance enhancers.",
  "tldr": "Illegal products containing SARMs and related drugs are sold for sport performance, often labelled as medicines or sold as supplements. Products from unregulated sources can contain unapproved drugs, sometimes unlabelled or at very high doses.",
  "methods": "OMCL laboratories collected retrospective and prospective data from January 2018 to September 2023 using a harmonised reporting template, with mainly LC-MS screening. Results were summarised as counts by origin, product type, dosage form, molecule and quantity.",
  "findings": "Of 336 reported samples, 12 had no in-scope active compound, leaving 324 samples; samples with more than one target compound gave 354 valid results. About 86% of samples came from the illegal supply chain, 65% of results were presented as medicines and 24% as dietary supplements. Eighteen molecules were detected, led by ibutamoren (62 reports), ligandrol (48), ostarine (46), cardarine (45) and andarine (34).",
  "limitations": "Only OMCL results were counted, so the number of circulating products is higher. Quantitative data were limited and reported in mixed units. Health outcomes in consumers were not measured.",
  "practicalImplications": "Products labelled as medicines or supplements can contain unapproved SARMs or other drugs, and dosing varied widely, including very high-dose liquids and high-purity powders for self-dosing. The authors advise against buying these products from suspected websites that hide a physical address.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Unregulated products marketed for muscle gain or performance often lack ingredient labels and vary widely in dose. The study did not assess any performance effect.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it describes product contents and does not assess injury, recovery or clinical outcomes in athletes."
 },

   "tldr/athleteDev: 'unknown ingredients' overstated; labelled contents matched analysis in about 88% of labelled samples -> unapproved drugs, sometimes unlabelled (48% labelled) or very high dose"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Eligibility is borderline: a product-surveillance study with no athlete participants, kept as INCLUDE because the products were bought as sport performance enhancers. Minor internal inconsistency: '209 of the 356 results (81.5%)'.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

  "doi": "10.3390/idr15040043",
  "abstract": "Retrospective cohort of 1,283 male players in Serie A and LaLiga over two seasons, comparing players who had SARS-CoV-2 in 2020-21 with those who did not, using muscle injury counts from a public database.",
  "tldr": "Professional footballers who had COVID-19 in the 2020-21 season had about three to five times the hazard of muscle injury that season. The authors argue infection should be treated as a return-to-play concern that needs specific assessment.",
  "methods": "Retrospective cohort of Serie A and LaLiga players, using Transfermarkt injury, match and minute data. Players were grouped by infection in 2020-21 and compared with t tests, multiple linear regression and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, following STROBE and CHAMP guidance.",

  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest infection history should be part of return-to-play decisions, with specific muscle assessment and training rather than only symptom resolution. They call for further study of tailored rehabilitation after infection.",

  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The authors recommend that return-to-play decisions after SARS-CoV-2 include specific muscle assessment and training, not only symptom remission and drug cessation. The study cannot set a return-to-play timeline or show that these steps reduce injury."
 },

{
 "id": "Q20",
 "sourceFile": "SPEEDI~1.PDF",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics and Limb Loading During Split-Belt Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL Reconstruction', matches the truncated filename SPEEDI~1.PDF.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": [
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
  "Sports Medicine & Injury"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Rehabilitation",
  "Sports Medicine"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Controlled laboratory study in 24 people 6 to 12 months after ACL reconstruction (15 female, 9 male), walking on a split-belt treadmill with the operated-leg belt set at 30% to 170% of 1.1 m/s in eight randomised 5-minute conditions. Faster operated-leg speeds increased early-stance knee moments and vertical loads, while slower speeds lowered early peaks and raised midstance loading. The authors report a dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee and limb loading.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The study examines acute single-session effects with 2-minute washouts, so aftereffects and training effects were not tested. Participants were not described as athletes, and they did not show the baseline loading asymmetry the authors expected.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the split-belt result as a proven way to correct underloading after ACL reconstruction, when the study measured only acute gait changes during one treadmill session.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Johnson AK, Recchia R, Tayfur A, Krishnan C, Palmieri-Smith RM. Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics and Limb Loading During Split-Belt Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL Reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2025:1-9.",
  "doi": "10.1177/03635465251365035",
  "abstract": "Controlled laboratory study of 24 people after ACL reconstruction walking on a split-belt treadmill, with the operated-leg belt set at eight speeds from 30% to 170% of 1.1 m/s.",
  "tldr": "Changing the speed of the operated-leg belt changes knee and limb loading in a graded way. Faster speeds raised early-stance loading and slower speeds raised midstance loading, so the speed chosen matters.",
  "methods": "Participants walked on an instrumented split-belt treadmill with 3D motion capture. After a tied-belt baseline at 1.1 m/s, eight 5-minute decoupled-speed conditions were run in random order, with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between them. Knee moments, angles and vertical ground-reaction forces were compared with baseline using statistical parametric mapping.",
  "findings": "Operated-leg speeds of 130% to 170% generally increased early-stance peak loads, while 30% and 50% decreased them. Slower speeds (30% to 90%) raised midstance knee moment and vertical load, and faster speeds lowered them. Linear models fitted most relationships, which the authors describe as dose-response.",
  "limitations": "Participants did not show the expected baseline loading asymmetry. The 2-minute washout may not have cleared prior effects, although speeds were randomised. Most participants had patellar tendon grafts, and the design cannot show aftereffects or transfer to overground walking.",
  "practicalImplications": "Split-belt speed is a dose that can be set to raise or lower knee and limb loading during treadmill walking. The authors suggest slower (30% to 50%) or faster (150% to 170%) operated-leg speeds as options to explore, not as proven protocols.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: No performance outcome was measured. The findings concern loading during rehabilitation walking only.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study suggests split-belt speed can change knee loading during rehabilitation, but it cannot show that the effect lasts after training or transfers to overground walking or return to sport. The acute loading changes should not be used as a return-to-sport criterion."
 }
}

1	Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of
2	Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics
3	and Limb Loading During Split-Belt
4	Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL
5	Reconstruction
6	Alexa K. Johnson,* PhD, Reagan Recchia,* BS, Abdulhamit Tayfur,*y PT, PhD,
7	Chandramouli Krishnan,z§||{# PT, PhD, and Riann M. Palmieri-Smith,*#** ATC, PhD
8	Investigation performed at University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
9	
10	Background: Surgical limb underloading is a common biomechanical adaptation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
11	(ACLR) and has been linked to early degenerative changes in knee cartilage, which are considered precursors to posttraumatic
12	osteoarthritis. Split-belt treadmill training is an emerging rehabilitation approach that modifies load through asymmetric gait
13	behavior, in which one limb walks faster than the other. While previous research has indicated that split-belt treadmill training
14	can modify limb loading, its effects on post-ACLR biomechanics remain unexplored.
15	Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of decoupling speed on knee biomechanics and limb
16	loading and model their relationship. It was hypothesized that at faster decoupling speeds, knee loads would increase, and at
17	slower speeds, they would decrease.
18	Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
19	Methods: Knee joint biomechanics were evaluated while 24 participants (15 females; mean age, 23.5 6 6.5 years; mean height,
20	1.72 6 0.08 m; mean mass, 75.61 6 13.83 kg; mean postoperative time, 7.94 6 1.74 months) with ACLR walked on an instru-
21	mented treadmill (2000 Hz) synced with a 12-camera motion capture system (200 Hz). Participants completed 5 minutes of base-
22	line walking at 1.1 m/s on tied treadmill belts. Afterward, the authors manipulated the speed of the belt under the ACL-
23	reconstructed leg with 8 randomized 5-minute decoupled speed configurations (ACL-reconstructed limb at 30%-170% of
24	1.1 m/s in 20% increments) with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between each speed. Bilateral sagittal plane knee moments,
25	angles, and vertical ground-reaction forces were calculated. Statistical parametric mapping was used to evaluate the effects
26	of decoupling speed on the dependent variables during the stance phase of the gait.
27	Results: A clear dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee/limb loading was found. Specifically, faster de-
28	coupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1m/s) generally increased peak loads and slower speeds (30% and 50% of 1.1 m/s) decreased
29	peak loads during early stance compared with tied-belt walking for both limbs. In contrast, slower decoupling speeds (30%-90% of
30	1.1 m/s) led to higher bilateral knee/limb loads at midstance, while faster decoupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1 m/s) resulted in
31	less knee/limb loading during midstance.
32	Conclusion: These findings suggest that split-belt treadmill training offers a promising method for modulating knee/limb loading
33	post-ACLR.
34	Clinical Relevance: Split-belt treadmill training could be a viable intervention to target the loading asymmetry that is prevalent in
35	persons post-ACLR.
36	Keywords: knee; rehabilitation; gait retraining; asymmetry

Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of
Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics
and Limb Loading During Split-Belt
Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL
Reconstruction
Alexa K. Johnson,* PhD, Reagan Recchia,* BS, Abdulhamit Tayfur,*y PT, PhD,
Chandramouli Krishnan,z§||{# PT, PhD, and Riann M. Palmieri-Smith,*#** ATC, PhD
Investigation performed at University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA

Background: Surgical limb underloading is a common biomechanical adaptation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
(ACLR) and has been linked to early degenerative changes in knee cartilage, which are considered precursors to posttraumatic
osteoarthritis. Split-belt treadmill training is an emerging rehabilitation approach that modifies load through asymmetric gait
behavior, in which one limb walks faster than the other. While previous research has indicated that split-belt treadmill training
can modify limb loading, its effects on post-ACLR biomechanics remain unexplored.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of decoupling speed on knee biomechanics and limb
loading and model their relationship. It was hypothesized that at faster decoupling speeds, knee loads would increase, and at
slower speeds, they would decrease.
Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
Methods: Knee joint biomechanics were evaluated while 24 participants (15 females; mean age, 23.5 6 6.5 years; mean height,
1.72 6 0.08 m; mean mass, 75.61 6 13.83 kg; mean postoperative time, 7.94 6 1.74 months) with ACLR walked on an instru-
mented treadmill (2000 Hz) synced with a 12-camera motion capture system (200 Hz). Participants completed 5 minutes of base-
line walking at 1.1 m/s on tied treadmill belts. Afterward, the authors manipulated the speed of the belt under the ACL-
reconstructed leg with 8 randomized 5-minute decoupled speed configurations (ACL-reconstructed limb at 30%-170% of
1.1 m/s in 20% increments) with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between each speed. Bilateral sagittal plane knee moments,
angles, and vertical ground-reaction forces were calculated. Statistical parametric mapping was used to evaluate the effects
of decoupling speed on the dependent variables during the stance phase of the gait.
Results: A clear dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee/limb loading was found. Specifically, faster de-
coupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1m/s) generally increased peak loads and slower speeds (30% and 50% of 1.1 m/s) decreased
peak loads during early stance compared with tied-belt walking for both limbs. In contrast, slower decoupling speeds (30%-90% of
1.1 m/s) led to higher bilateral knee/limb loads at midstance, while faster decoupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1 m/s) resulted in
less knee/limb loading during midstance.
Conclusion: These findings suggest that split-belt treadmill training offers a promising method for modulating knee/limb loading
post-ACLR.
Clinical Relevance: Split-belt treadmill training could be a viable intervention to target the loading asymmetry that is prevalent in
persons post-ACLR.
Keywords: knee; rehabilitation; gait retraining; asymmetry

15	Abstract
16	Carnosine levels play a significant role in intracellular pH buffering during exercise. The limiting factor for muscle carno-
17	sine synthesis is the availability of β-alanine. Results from meta-analysis showed a significant positive effect of β-alanine
18	supplementation on high-intensity exercise performance. Nonetheless, much less has been described about the safety of
19	β-alanine. The available literature indicates no adverse events related to β-alanine usage; side effects such as paresthesia
20	may be observed if a large single high dose of β-alanine is taken, but the symptom can be attenuated either by using splitting
21	doses (< 1.6 g) or a sustained-release formula. No adverse effects have been reported up to 24 weeks of β-alanine supple-
22	mentation (3.2 g.day−1), but the adverse effects of longer supplementation periods are still unknown. Most of the existing
23	clinical studies were not designed with safety evaluations as primary end points. β-Alanine is currently considered to be safe
24	in healthy populations, at recommended doses, by the International Society of Sports Nutrition stands position, while the
25	Australian Institute of Sports has established β-alanine as a safe performance-enhancing supplement with strong scientific
26	evidence (grade A). Cohort studies are needed evaluating the safety of β-alanine among representative populations, and the
27	effects of co-variables such as sex, age, and ethnicity.

    REVIEW



Safety of beta‑alanine supplementation in humans: a narrative review
Erick P. de Oliveira1 · Guilherme G. Artioli2 · Roberto Carlos Burini3

Received: 12 June 2022 / Accepted: 8 February 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag Italia S.r.l., part of Springer Nature 2023


Abstract
Carnosine levels play a significant role in intracellular pH buffering during exercise. The limiting factor for muscle carno-
sine synthesis is the availability of β-alanine. Results from meta-analysis showed a significant positive effect of β-alanine
supplementation on high-intensity exercise performance. Nonetheless, much less has been described about the safety of
β-alanine. The available literature indicates no adverse events related to β-alanine usage; side effects such as paresthesia
may be observed if a large single high dose of β-alanine is taken, but the symptom can be attenuated either by using splitting
doses (< 1.6 g) or a sustained-release formula. No adverse effects have been reported up to 24 weeks of β-alanine supple-
mentation (3.2 g.day−1), but the adverse effects of longer supplementation periods are still unknown. Most of the existing
clinical studies were not designed with safety evaluations as primary end points. β-Alanine is currently considered to be safe
in healthy populations, at recommended doses, by the International Society of Sports Nutrition stands position, while the
Australian Institute of Sports has established β-alanine as a safe performance-enhancing supplement with strong scientific
evidence (grade A). Cohort studies are needed evaluating the safety of β-alanine among representative populations, and the
effects of co-variables such as sex, age, and ethnicity.

Keywords Safety · Adverse events · Side effects · Exercise · Performance

Abstract
   As the NFL's salary cap has surged from $34 million in 1994 to $255 million in 2024, effective cap
management has become crucial. However, relatively little focus has been paid to how spending on spe-
cific positions affects team success. The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between
salary cap allocation and team success in the NFL, specifically focusing on how spending in different
positions affects win percentage. We utilized a quantitative design, analyzing 384 NFL team observations
from the 2013–2024 seasons, with linear regression models applied to assess how salary cap allocations
across key positions impacted team success, using win percentage as the primary outcome variable and
the number of wins as a robustness check. Our findings show that higher spending on quarterbacks, wide
receivers, and offensive linemen is strongly linked to improved team performance, while expenditures
on running backs and tight ends have little to no significant impact. These results suggest that teams
could benefit from reallocating resources to more critical positions, particularly quarterbacks and wide
receivers, to maximize on-field performance. This study also offers practical insights for NFL teams
seeking to refine their salary cap strategies.


Keywords: salary dispersion, positional spending, team success, National Football League

  "limitations": "The authors report heterogeneity in methods, populations and assays, few power analyses, underrepresentation of women, and mostly quasi-experimental designs with a single post-stressor measure.",
  "practicalImplications": "Saliva osmolality, total protein and flow rate are the most consistent hydration signals in the review, so they are the best-supported field candidates for now. Cortisol and testosterone need baseline and diurnal control before they can support readiness decisions.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Salivary hydration markers may help monitor hydration around training. The review found no consistent link between cortisol or testosterone and performance outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review covers stress and readiness rather than injury recovery, so it cannot inform return to sport. Its muscle-damage markers were reported in single studies with varying timelines, so they cannot guide return decisions."

General Characteristics. Details and key findings extracted from the included studies are reported in Fig 2 and
S3 Table. A majority (67%) of the research was conducted in the USA, Australia, and the United Kingdom. Most (71%)
were published within the last 10 years and none were older than 20 years. The average sample size of the included
studies was 23 out of a total 1,118 participants across all studies with ages in included samples ranging from 18–52
years. A diverse range of participants were represented in the included articles (Fig 2A), with 9 studies involving military
participants [17,33,49–55], as well as a variety testing athletes of sports like rugby [56–60], soccer [61–65], running
[66–68], rock climbers [69,70], weight-lifting [71,72], and cycling [20,73–75] amongst other sports [76,77]. Many also
simply tested healthy adults [1,18,19,78–85]. In addition, 2 studies considered emergency physicians and investigated the
exposure of health care personnel to acute stressors and possible implications on their performance and decision making
[86,87]. However, of the 49 studies, only 13 included both sexes, with a total of 194 males and 101 females in these
studies.
    Experimental methodology. Details on the designs, measured biomarkers, performance measures, and key findings
are reported in S3 Table. Twenty-two out of the 49 studies were prospective cohort studies in that they attempted
to describe how salivary markers change in response to stressors that are seen in a naturalistic setting but lacked
comparative control groups [17,33,49–51,53,54,57–60,64–66,68,70,77,86–90]. Twelve studies were quasi-experimental
in that the researchers measured response to imposed stressors pre-post [19,67,69,71,74,76,78,79,82,83,85,91]. Eleven

true control group [92]. Three of the studies reported a predictive model of a participant’s outcome based on levels of

significantly increased during the 3-day recovery period compared to baseline in one study due to stressors that included
military training, exercise, and sleep deprivation [53] while it increased in another due to survival training associated
[54]. Lieberman et al. reported a decrease in morning levels of cortisol but an increase in evening levels due to intense
exercise with load carriage, sleep deprivation, dehydration, and heat environmental stressors [33]. Another study did
not provide specific quantitative concentration levels of cortisol but found an association between cortisol levels and
performance ratings by coaches and players [90]. Several studies reported that testosterone [33,53] and T:C ratio
[53] decreased in response to military training, exercise, sleep deprivation, and heat environment stressors. Taylor
et al. discovered that DHEA-s levels increased during both the morning and afternoon, while the DHEA-s to cortisol
ratio exhibited an increase in the morning and a decrease in the evening. [54]. The digestive enzyme alpha-amylase
was shown to increase shortly before, and then significantly decrease 1 day after a Taekwondo competition relative to
baseline [77]. Fogt et al. reported that osmolality increased while total protein concentration decreased in Air Force basic
military trainees due to exercise and dehydration stressors [52]. In one study, a proteomic and metabolomic analysis
identified clusters of proteins and metabolites capable of distinguishing between various states of combat missions [51].
Additionally, another study identified clusters of metabolites associated with cognitive performance and their ability to
differentiate between groups based on their sleep patterns [76]. A single study examined melatonin response to intense
exercise with load carriage, sleep deprivation, dehydration, and heat environment stressors and found no change in
that were well correlated with serum markers of oxidate stress [99].
    Innovative approaches involving proteomics and metabolomics have identified promising markers for fatigue detection.
For instance, a panel of five proteins (e.g., periplakin, heat shock protein alpha family B member 9, myeloperoxidase,
heat shock protein family A member 9, and transketolase) discriminated between fatigued and non-fatigued individuals
with 83% accuracy following military training, while a panel of 5 metabolites (e.g., C16H13-ClN2O, gamma-butyrobetaine,
L-proline, proline-glycine, and pipecolic acid) achieved 96% accuracy in discriminating fatigue status in the same sample
[51]. The identified molecules associated with innate immunity, protein cycling and processing, and metabolism of sugars
and amino acids, were identified using a discovery approach in which samples were analyzed using mass spectrometry to
quantify all detectable proteins and/or metabolites. From which a subset that best predicted fatigue status was identified
using statistical techniques like linear discriminant analysis (LDA) [51] and Fisher discriminant analysis [86]. Other recent
evidence supports the use of the proteome to evaluate physical stress as proteins linked to immune response, antioxidant

Limitations
There are several limitations of the available literature. Although a majority of the included articles (55%) were scored as
‘good’ quality via the Downs and Black checklist, a large portion (45%) were only rated as ‘fair’ quality with most articles



PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                       18 / 27
 scoring poorly on external validity and control of confounding factors. This reflects the largely quasi-experimental nature of
the included, with most using non-random sampling plans and group assignments.
    Heterogeneity in study populations, methodological designs, and biomarkers examined further limits the generalizability
of findings. For instance, the effects observed on testosterone levels following mid-week rugby training [88] may not be
directly comparable to those from a 21-day cycling training protocol [74], despite both being stressful physical activities
potentially inducing muscle damage. Broad methodological shortcomings also include an insufficient consideration of
baseline conditions, such as failing to account for diurnal variations in hormone levels before assessing stressor impacts.
Additionally, many studies only take a single post-stressor measurement, which does not adequately capture the dura-
tion of the stressor’s effects. Furthermore, analyses often aggregate data at the group level, which may obscure the wide
range of individual differences in biochemical responses.
    A more specific methodological limitation was variations in assay designs may significantly impact the measurement
and interpretation of biomarker availability across studies. Differences in detection methods, such as enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assays (ELISA) versus radioimmunoassays (RIA), influence sensitivity and specificity. For example,
ELISA, commonly used in many studies, are scalable and suitable for a broad range of concentrations but can exhibit vari-
able sensitivity depending on assay design [155]. RIA offers superior sensitivity for measuring hormones that are present

{
 "id": "Q24",
 "sourceFile": "Same-year repeat concussions in the National Football League - Trends from 2015-through 2019.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'Same-Year Repeat Concussions in the National Football League: Trends from 2015 through 2019', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "American Football"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Injured Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective observational cohort of NFL players with football-related concussions in the 2015 to 2019 seasons, drawn from the league's electronic health records. Same-year repeat concussion occurred in 0.38% to 0.69% of all players per season and in 5.3% to 8.3% of players with a concussion. Players with a repeat concussion missed a median of 12 days, against 9 days after a single concussion.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Data come from one league with no player-game exposure measure, and limits placed on players after clearance were not captured. The file is a pre-proof, so the final text and figures may change.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the similar repeat and single-concussion rates as proof that return-to-play protocols make players safe, when the study can show neither causation nor exposure.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Cools M, Zuckerman S, Herzog M, Mack C, Lee RY, et al. Same-Year Repeat Concussions in the National Football League: Trends from 2015 through 2019. World Neurosurgery. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.wneu.2022.02.033",
  "abstract": "Retrospective study of NFL concussions in 2015 to 2019 that measured the risk of a second concussion in the same NFL year, the time between injuries and return-to-play time.",
  "tldr": "Once players were back, a second concussion in the same NFL year was about as likely as a first. Repeat concussions were followed by longer time out, which supports careful return-to-play review.",
  "methods": "Retrospective observational cohort of all NFL players with concussions in 2015 to 2019, drawn from the league's electronic health records. Rates were calculated per season, missed and participation days were compared with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and risk ratios were estimated with log-binomial regression.",
  "findings": "Same-year repeat concussion occurred in 0.38% to 0.69% of all players per season and in 5.3% to 8.3% of concussed players, similar to the single-concussion risk. The median number of participation days between injuries was 38. Median missed time was 12 days after a repeat concussion, against 9 days after a single concussion (p less than 0.0001).",
  "limitations": "Single-league data with no player-exposure denominator and no account of limits set after clearance. Few repeat events limited subgroup analysis. The abstract calls the design case-control while the Methods describe a cohort. The Discussion gives a single-concussion range of 6.2% to 8.0%, against 6.2% to 8.3% in Table 1. The Conclusion links more missed time to higher repeat risk, but the reported result (RR 1.48, 95% CI 0.94 to 2.31) was not significant.",
  "practicalImplications": "Players cleared under the current protocols showed a repeat risk similar to the single-concussion risk. Longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review, though the association was not significant.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The paper does not measure performance. Its use is in planning season-level risk and availability after concussion.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study supports careful, staged return-to-play protocols, since cleared players had a repeat risk similar to the single-concussion risk. It cannot show that the protocol caused that result, and longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review."
 }
}

138	Introduction
139	       Increasing knowledge and awareness surrounding sport-related concussion (SRC) in
140	recent decades has resulted in concerted efforts directed toward reducing repeat SRC rates.
141	Repeat or recurrent concussions have been associated with a slower recovery,1 depression,2 sleep
142	disturbances,3 late-life cognitive impairment,4 and longer return-to-play (RTP) times compared
143	to first-time injuries.5,6,7 Though many studies have evaluated the risk of repeat SRC throughout
144	an athlete’s career,2,4,8–10 few have delved into the incidence of same-year repeat concussions,
145	especially among elite American football players.
146	       A previous study reviewed concussions in the National Football League (NFL) between
147	
148	                                                             of
149	1996 and 2001 and reported a 5.5% rate of same-season repeat concussions.11 A follow-up study
150	found a similar risk of repeat concussions between two time periods of the 1996-2001 vs. 2002-
151	                                                       ro
152	2007 seasons (24.7% vs. 24.2%).11 Although the second follow-up study did not restrict the
153	                                                 -p
154	definition of repeat concussion to same-year repeat concussion, the authors found that 90% of
155	
156	                                           re
157	repeat concussions occurred more than 28 days after the initial concussion. The average time
158	between concussions was 456 days, signifying most injuries likely occurred in different
159	seasons.11                         lP
160	                            na

162	implemented in the NFL in recent years.12–14 With respect to RTP, players must pass a series of
163	                      ur
164	clinical qualifications to be cleared for play. From 2015-2019, between 283-302 concussions
165	
166	               Jo
167	were reported per year (offseason through the postseason) in the NFL.15 The most recent
168	publication regarding same-year repeat concussion in the NFL is from 1996-2001;16 more recent
169	data is needed to fully understand the current scope of same-year repeat concussion.
170	       In the current study, we sought to: 1) report the risk of same-year repeat concussions in
171	the NFL, 2) describe the time pattern of when same-year repeat concussions occur, and 3)
172	present RTP time and intervening time between same-year repeat concussions. Given recent
173	evidence-based changes in concussion management, the staged approach for RTP, and plateaued
174	rates of SRC due to increased awareness and prevention measures,15 we would expect the risk of

211

214	through mid-March and is denoted by the initial year. The year begins with an offseason program
215	and progresses in order of preseason, regular season, and postseason. An initial concussion was
216	defined as the first concussion in a player who sustained a same-year repeat concussion. A player
217	with a single concussion was defined as a player who had only one concussion during the full
218	NFL year (no subsequent concussions in that same year).

220	SRCs. RTP was defined as the time when the athlete had fully cleared concussion protocol and
221	was released to full-contact practice and games. Any limitations placed on a player meant they

import json
d=json.load(open('drafts/Q24.json'))
p=d['paper']

Players with a repeat concussion missed a median of 12 days, against 9 days after a single concussion."

p['tldr']="Among NFL players who had a concussion, the chance of a second one in the same NFL year was about the same as any player's chance of a first. Repeat concussions were followed by longer time out, and about 1 in 5 repeats came within two weeks of return."
p['findings']="Same-year repeat concussion occurred in 0.38% to 0.69% of all players per season and in 5.3% to 8.3% of concussed players, similar to the one-season risk of any concussion among all players (6.2% to 8.3%). The median number of participation days between injuries was 38, and 18.8% of repeats occurred within two weeks of return. Median missed time was 12 days after a repeat concussion, against 9 days after a single concussion (p less than 0.0001)."
p['practicalImplications']="Players cleared under the current protocols had a same-year repeat risk similar to the league-wide risk of a first concussion. Longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review, though the association was not significant."
p['rtp']="Return to Sport Application: Cleared players had a same-year repeat risk similar to the league-wide risk of any concussion, which is consistent with, but does not prove, adequate recovery before return under staged protocols. The study has no comparison protocol and cannot show cause, and longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review."
p['limitations']=p['limitations']+" The comparator for the repeat risk is the risk of any concussion among all players, and no formal test of that comparison is shown in the Results. Two authors are affiliated with the NFL."
d['verification']={"status":"CORRECTED","changes":[
"paper.citation: author list stopped at 5 -> 6 authors before et al. (Solomon G added)",
"evidenceSummary/findings/practicalImplications/tldr: comparator called 'single-concussion risk' -> one-season risk of any concussion among all players ('This was similar to the risk of sustaining any concussion, which ranged from 6.2% (2018) to 8.3% (2017)'); added 18.8% of repeats within two weeks of return",
"paper.rtp: 'The study supports careful, staged return-to-play protocols' implied protocol effect -> consistent with but does not prove adequate recovery; no comparison protocol",
"paper.limitations: added comparator and untested-comparison note and NFL author affiliation"],
"residualConcerns":"Concussion and return-to-play topic. Pre-proof text; two authors (Solomon, Sills) are NFL-affiliated and the Conclusion describes the protocol as effective without a comparison group.",
"spotCheckPriority":"high"}
json.dump(d,open('verified/Q24.json','w'),indent=1,ensure_ascii=False)
EOF
